name: Pale black
lede: Pale black is a dark reddish-brown filed under a traditional Japanese color name, Binrōjizome, "betel nut dyed."

sections.title: A betel-nut dye
sections.body:
Our library lists this swatch as *Binrōjizome* (檳榔子染), which translates as "betel nut dyed," one of the traditional colors of Japan recorded on Wikipedia's list of that name [1]. The English label "Pale black" is this app's own rendering of the name, not a separate historical term, and the dye plant or source behind the Japanese name is not further documented in the sources checked here [1]. Its nearest named neighbor in our data is [[pale-black-tone]], only 2.8 units off, essentially the same color on screen [2]; [[zulu]] sits 3.2 units away.

Despite its name, the swatch reads as a warm, dark brown rather than true black, close to [[woodland-brown]] and [[chocolate-brown]] in hue [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a color within range of this swatch in 3,316 of 23,781 paintings, 13.94 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens, requiring real coverage, finds it in 2,803 [3]. That makes it more common than 98 percent of the named colors in our library [3]. It most often plays a mid-tone, in 44 percent of those 2,803 paintings by lightness rank, so varnish cannot fake the result [3].

Eastman Johnson is its most devoted painter, present in 6 of his 18 works here, 3.3 times the expected rate for the museums those paintings come from [3]. The earliest match dates to the year 1119, centuries before any dyed textile using this name could have existed, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3].
